Chinese Massage Techniques: A Guide to Common Methods

Chinese massage uses a diverse range of techniques. Learn the most common methods and what they treat.

Overview of Chinese Massage Techniques

Chinese massage — most commonly known as Tui Na (推拿) — is a hands-on therapeutic system rooted in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM). Unlike Western massage modalities that focus primarily on soft tissue relaxation, Chinese massage techniques target the body’s meridian network to regulate qi (vital energy) and blood flow.

The name “Tui Na” itself describes two of its foundational movements: Tui (push) and Na (grasp). But a complete session draws from a repertoire of at least eight distinct chinese massage techniques, each selected and sequenced based on the patient’s diagnosis. A practitioner may use a gentle rubbing motion to warm an area, then switch to deep sustained pressure on an acupoint, followed by joint rotations to increase range of motion.

This guide walks through each major technique, what it feels like on the receiving end, and how they combine into a full treatment session. If you are new to TCM bodywork, start with our overview of Chinese massage to understand the foundational principles first.

Tui (Push) — Meridian Stroke

Tui is a rhythmic pushing motion performed with the thumb, palm, or thenar eminence along the line of a meridian. The practitioner applies moderate pressure while gliding forward, then releases and repeats. Think of it as a broad, sweeping stroke — slower than effleurage in Swedish massage and always aligned with the direction of qi flow prescribed by TCM theory.

What it feels like: A warm, spreading sensation as the practitioner’s hand moves in one continuous direction. You will not feel deep digging like a trigger-point release; Tui is designed to move energy rather than break up adhesions. Sessions often begin with Tui to open the meridians and prepare the tissue for deeper work.

Na (Grasp) — Muscle Kneading

Na involves grasping, lifting, squeezing, and rolling the muscle belly between the thumb and fingers — similar to petrissage in Western massage but performed with a specific TCM intention. The practitioner grips a handful of muscle, lifts it away from the bone, kneads it, and releases.

What it feels like: A satisfying deep squeeze, often on the trapezius, deltoids, or forearms. You might notice the practitioner uses alternating hands in a “milking” motion down the length of the muscle. Na is commonly used on limbs and shoulders to relieve muscle tension, improve local circulation, and disperse stagnation.

An (Press) — Acupressure

An is stationary, perpendicular pressure applied with the thumb, finger, elbow, or knuckle directly onto an acupoint (acupressure point). The practitioner locates a point along the meridian, sinks into it gradually, and holds the pressure for 15–60 seconds — sometimes with a subtle circular oscillation.

What it feels like: A distinct “deqi” sensation — sometimes described as dull ache, heaviness, or a mild electrical tingling that radiates along the meridian path. This is the hallmark of successful acupressure. Unlike the “good pain” of a deep tissue massage, An produces a more targeted, almost medicinal awareness at the point.

A 2018 systematic review in Annals of Internal Medicine (PubMed) found that acupressure reduced lower back pain more effectively than physical therapy alone, though the authors noted larger trials are needed.

Mo (Rub) — Circular Friction

Mo is a light circular rubbing motion performed with the palm or fingertips. The skin moves with the hand rather than the hand sliding over the skin. The pressure is gentle — just enough to generate warmth and friction at the surface level.

What it feels like: Comforting and grounding. Mo is often used on the abdomen, lower back, or around joints where gentle heat is therapeutic. Practitioners use this chinese massage technique to regulate digestive function when applied to the abdomen (a common TCM approach for bloating or poor appetite).

Gun (Roll) — Deep Compression

Gun is a rolling motion in which the practitioner uses the back of their hand — specifically the dorsal side of the knuckles — to deliver a wave of compressive pressure across a broad area. The wrist remains loose, and the forearm rotates to produce a continuous rolling action, like a slow wheel traveling over the muscle.

What it feels like: Broad and heavier than Tui. You will feel the weight of the practitioner’s arm transferring through their hand into broader muscle groups — the back, glutes, and thighs are typical targets. Gun is excellent for reaching the intermediate muscle layer without the point-specific intensity of a thumb or elbow.

Cuo (Rub) — Heat Generation

Cuo is a fast, back-and-forth rubbing motion applied with both palms sandwiching a limb. The practitioner places one hand on each side of the arm or leg and moves them in opposite directions at high speed. This generates considerable friction heat.

What it feels like: A rapid, intense warmth that rises almost immediately. Cuo is often used at the end of a session on the arms or legs to “seal” the treatment — the TCM rationale is that it helps the body retain and integrate the qi that was moved during the earlier techniques. It is brief, typically lasting 30–60 seconds.

Dou (Shake) — Vibration

Dou is a quick shaking or trembling motion applied by the practitioner gripping the patient’s wrist or ankle and creating a fine, high-frequency oscillation that travels through the limb.

What it feels like: A buzz or flutter that travels through the joint and muscle. It is not forceful — the practitioner is not trying to stretch or manipulate the joint. Dou is used to release residual tension after deeper work and to calm the nervous system before the session ends. Patients often report feeling “looser” in the joints afterward even though the technique involves almost no pressure.

Yao (Rotate) & Ban (Pull) — Joint Mobilization

Yao involves passive rotation of a joint — typically the neck, shoulder, hip, or knee — through its natural range of motion. The practitioner cradles the limb or head and slowly guides it through circles, gradually expanding the arc.

Ban is a quick, controlled pulling motion applied to a joint after it has been positioned at its end-range through Yao. The practitioner executes a short-amplitude, high-velocity thrust — similar to chiropractic or osteopathic adjustments.

What it feels like: Yao is smooth and relaxing; you will feel the joint being moved in ways you may not actively stretch yourself. Ban produces a brief cavitation (the audible “pop” that is normal and harmless for healthy joints). These are advanced techniques best performed by practitioners with formal musculoskeletal training.

How Techniques Are Combined in a Session

A typical 60-minute Tui Na session does not use all eight techniques in equal measure. Practitioners sequence them based on the TCM diagnosis established during intake.

A common session structure looks like this:

  1. Open the channels — Tui and Mo (5–10 minutes) to warm tissue and assess response
  2. Deep work — Na, An, and Gun (25–35 minutes) targeting the affected meridians and muscle groups
  3. Joint release — Yao and Ban (10–15 minutes) if restrictions were identified
  4. Close and ground — Cuo and Dou (5 minutes) to settle the body and restore calm

The choice and emphasis of chinese massage techniques varies by condition. A patient with chronic neck tension might receive heavy Na and An work on GB-20 and GB-21 points, while someone recovering from a sports injury may get more Gun and Yao to restore mobility. Learn more about what conditions these techniques address in our benefits of Chinese massage guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Does Chinese massage hurt? A: Some techniques produce strong sensations — An (acupressure) creates a deep ache called deqi, and Ban (pull) may cause a quick pop. But Tui Na should never be intensely painful. If a technique feels sharp or bruising, tell your practitioner immediately.

Q: How is Chinese massage different from Swedish massage? A: Swedish massage uses long gliding strokes (effleurage) and kneading (petrissage) aimed at relaxation and superficial muscle tension. Chinese massage techniques target meridian lines and acupoints, use joint mobilization, and are driven by a TCM diagnosis rather than a fixed protocol.

Q: Do clothes stay on during a Tui Na session? A: Yes. Tui Na is performed through loose, comfortable clothing rather than directly on oiled skin. This is one of its practical advantages — no need to undress or clean off oil afterward.

Q: Can I see a Tui Na practitioner for an injury? A: Many people use Tui Na for musculoskeletal issues, but always consult a medical doctor for an injury diagnosis first. A qualified practitioner should work alongside — not replace — your primary healthcare provider.

Q: How long does it take to feel results? A: Some patients report immediate relief after the first session, especially for acute tension. Chronic conditions typically require a course of 6–12 sessions for sustained improvement.
